articles.title: Vote No on I-638 To Protect Me and My Teammates
articles.author: By Jillian
paras: I play varsity high school girls basketball, and if I were old enough to vote, I would vote NO to stop ballot Initiative 638 from passing this November.

To enforce excluding trans girls from sports, I-638 would require all girls to submit to sex inspections before being allowed to play any sport in elementary, middle, and high school. I outright reject claims by the MAGA mega-millionaire behind I-638, Brian Heywood, that this initiative is protecting my safety!

The people behind I-638 say they want to protect me from a tiny, vulnerable, and already bullied minority, transgender girls. I don’t need protection from my peers. I need to live in a community that includes, protects, and cares for all youth, regardless of gender identity.

True protection for female athletes would mean safeguards from some adult male coaches, who use their power to groom and abuse girls on their teams. It would also mean less interference from people who make fun of girls on the courts, comment on our bodies, and deny us the same equipment and access that boys have. Did you know that girls drop out of sports at higher rates than boys by age 14? A humiliating exam or testing that inflicts financial burdens on families —they will not be covered by insurance—will certainly affect girls’ participation in athletics now and for years to come!

To police all girls in sports, they want me to go through a new inspection during my sports physical to make sure I’m a girl by doing an invasive exam of my reproductive anatomy. Parents won’t be able to use our birth certificates to prove our sex.
Even little girls playing middle school sports (and some elementary school sports) will be examined. Boys who play sports are exempt from this new requirement. Tens of thousands of us girls are not.
Why are they putting us through this? To enforce a cruel ban, the most extreme of its kind in the nation, to keep a handful of trans girls from participating in athletics.

I’ve been playing basketball since 6th grade and I’ve never, to my knowledge, played with or against a trans girl. The Washington Interscholastic Athletic Association says there are just 5–10 trans children playing sports, out of 1.2 million students, so the chances are very small that I’ll ever encounter a trans girl on the court and if I did so what?

Sports are for everyone and we should be encouraging more people to seize the opportunity to get out and exercise and compete. My basketball teammates are my sisters. We laugh, pick each other up, disagree sometimes and support each other through challenges. They’ve taught me how to resolve conflicts, overcome frustration, and put my own ego aside for the sake of the team. Excluding trans girls from the benefits of friendship and teamwork only makes things worse for a small group of kids who already face higher violence and rates of suicide.

The people behind I-638 are using a scare tactic by saying a boy will claim to be a trans girl just to walk onto a girls’ team. Life is already hard enough for trans girls who strive to pass and belong. Even the Seattle Times calls the tactic “fearmongering.”

I-638 will discourage thousands of girls from participating in school sports, impacting the future of Washington girls’ sports for years to come. That’s the real danger to me and my teammates. I’m counting on all of you to vote against this harmful and exclusionary initiative.
Jillian is a high school basketball player from South Seattle. Her last name is withheld to protect her privacy.

paras: Been away for two weeks — happy to return to a packed inbox. Let’s get to the questions! — Dan

I’ve wavered on sending this but I need advice. There’s this woman I’ve known most of my life. We are very close and we have as close to an open book friendship as I can think of. We’ve shared everything. I now realize that I have romantic feelings for her that I never acted on. I’m 35, she’s 36. The wrinkle is that she’s now married with three small children. Our correspondence lately has recently gotten kind of flirtatious. I get the sense that she’s not happy in her marriage and I’m waiting for it to run its course. I want to be a supportive friend but I’m also interested in her in a way I’m almost certain she would reciprocate given the right circumstances, maybe years from now. What’s my best course of action here?

The fact that this woman seems unhappy in her marriage isn’t proof that 1. she’s actually unhappy (married people love to complain) or that 2. she’s unhappy enough to do something about it (current relationship satisfaction isn’t the only variable). Middle-aged, married, and responsible for small kids is an incredibly stressful stage of life, especially in a country that seems determined to make being a parent as difficult as possible. And as women in straight marriages still do more than their fair share of the household labor and childcare, straight married women have a lot to complain about. (Here’s hoping this woman’s husband is doing his fair share.) So, while this woman, like a lot of middle-aged moms, may fantasize about alternative timelines… timelines where she’s married to someone who helps out more and impregnates her less… it doesn’t follow that she would leave her husband to be with you or anyone else.

Zooming out: If your conversations with this woman were actually flirtatious (“kind of” flirtatious sounds like dickful thinking)… and if you knew for a fact that she was unhappy in her marriage (because she’d told you exactly that)… then I might encourage you to tell this woman how you feel. But unless and until things escalate — unless and until she starts saying things like “I wanna fuck you” and “I want out of my marriage” — there’s a good chance you’re reading things into your conversations with your old friend that are probably untrue. If things were to get unambiguous, PAIN, you could risk saying something to her. And if turns out she does want out of her marriage, knowing how you feel might encourage her to get out sooner. But unless and until things get unambiguous… unless and until it’s her telling you what you wanna hear, TITS, and not just your dick… your best course of action is to STFU.
P.S. Supportive friends don’t have ulterior motives.

I’m a bisexual married male. I came out to my spouse before I slept with a man for the first time, which I did with her permission. In the end I contracted a sexually transmitted infection during that first foray. I have a question about doxy and a follow-up question about gym etiquette. (I can’t really ask my doctor because I live in Texas.) How soon after a sexual encounter should I take my doxy? I think my mishap was due to me misunderstanding the directions. Which leads me to my gym question: I joined the gym for community more than anything else. I am not happy with my body, but it seems as though my body won’t be holding me back. I have been propositioned a few times and I love feeling desired by other men like this! I’ve heard stories about sexual things happening in the showers at the gym, but I don’t know whether this sort of thing is officially okay. Is messing around in the showers or the sauna actually okay?

1. Doxy directions aren’t that complicated, TITS, and they’re easily googled . But I’m here to help: Take your 200 mg dose of doxycycline as soon as possible after you have sex with another man — ideally within 24 hours, but no later than 72 hours — but don’t take more than 200 mg in any 24-hour period. (So, if you have sex with some dude in the morning and take your doxy immediately after, TITS, don’t take another round of doxy if you have sex with some other dude in that night.) Taking doxy greatly reduces your risk of contracting (and passing along) syphilis and chlamydia; it also reduces your risk of catching/spreading gonorrhea. You should also be on PrEP , which will protect you from HIV. And if you can’t talk to your doctor about these things, TITS, you need a different/better doctor.

2. A gym is not a sex club, TITS, so it’s not okay — officially — to mess around with other guys at the gym. But the stories you’ve heard aren’t urban legends: unlike men putting gerbils in their asses (a fading urban legend that’s just had new life breathed into it ), out gay and bi men have been known to mess around at gyms in urban gay neighborhoods . (Closet cases, on the other hand, mess around at gyms near suburban megachurches.) For many men, the fact that it’s not okay — because a gym is not a sex club — is part of the thrill. Guys who are indiscreet, careless, and sloppy about messing around at the gym get their memberships revoked.
P.S. If you actually wanted to cancel your gym membership — something most gyms make nearly impossible — getting “caught” messing around at the gym may be the best way to do it.

P.P.S. To learn the difference between friendly smile-and-nod eye contact at the gym and come-join-me-in-the-sauna-after-this-set eye contact at the gym, get your hands on a copy of Leo Herrera’s (Analogue) Cruising: A Manual .

I’m a 24-year-old woman married to a 27-year-old man. We’ve been together about six years and our sex life has always been off. He was a virgin when we met, and I struggled with low libido for a few years due to a hormone issue that has been fixed. He was the opposite: he wanted to bang nearly every day. paras: States fold in Paramount-Warner Bros merger lawsuit, broadcast media will consolidate under Trump ally: The twelve states suing to stop the creation of a broadcast media monopoly allied to the president decided actually, it’s OK, announcing a settlement Monday greenlighting the merger. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said in a press release that the settlement secured “significant concessions” to anti-competitive practices, none of which, I might add, address the underlying problem of one of the president’s top allies concentrating control over much of the television news and entertainment landscape, which Brown did not mention.

Why not just make an electric jet? In case you have not been following the story via your father’s subscription to Aviation Week & Space Technology , there’s a very accessible new Seattle Times story on California startup JetZero’s attempt to challenge Boeing’s domestic aerospace manufacturing dominance with a fat new airplane.. The innovative engineering is the “blended-wing” body shape of the proposed aircraft, which has never flown, with the innovative selling point being the better gas mileage the design provides. Personally I am skeptical of an unproven airframe manufactured by a new company to fill a very specific market niche, but JetZero has plenty of your tax dollars from the US Air Force to live off of while they figure out how to get off the ground.

US Sen. Susan Collins investigated for corruption: The FBI appears to have Maine’s Republican US senator dead to rights on taking bribes in the form of election campaign contributions from a shipbuilder in exchange for funneling federal contracts in the company’s direction. “It was eye-opening for me, frankly. Oh my God, all of it is for sale. It’s all for sale,” a former executive with the shipbuilding firm told ProPublica . So why isn’t Sen. Collins being prosecuted? Trump was reelected, and purged the FBI’s anti-corruption team. Collins is up for reelection, but considering her earlier opponent was a former mercenary with a Nazi tattoo who dropped out after sexual assault allegations surfaced, something normal like corruption might be the least of voters worries.

US Rep. Lauren Boebert investigated for bisexuality: A complaint filed with the US House Committee on Ethics last Thursday accuses the Colorado Republican of having sex with three House employees under her direct supervision and paying to keep them quiet. This includes two women, which in conservative culture is considered a bit of a faux pas if I am reading these reports correctly. Boebert, a noted bigot, has denied the allegations , which came from the political operative who previously accused her of being a sex worker, a claim news media could not independently corroborate. Boebert was, however, caught red-handed fondling that guy’s junk during a musical production of Beetlejuice . She’s also up for reelection.

HEARTWARMING! Ichiro demolishes arrogant high school girls: The nefarious high school girls All-Star team of Japan thought they could pull a fast one on the old man, and were rewarded with a 127-pitch shutout thrown by Ichiro, who was primarily an outfielder not a pitcher, the Seattle Times reports .

JPMorgan throws in the towel on forecasting a way out of America’s oil war: While gas prices are rising, prices haven’t been in total free fall for a few reasons even as the US, Iran, Israel, Yemen, Ukraine and Russia continue down the path of radical decarbonization. The Chinese cutting oil imports and falling back on their massive rainy day reserves saved the global economy for a while, and market analysts didn’t panic too much over the summer because they thought conventional wisdom of don’t do this shit would prevail. But this is the Trump administration, and so JPMorgan had to announce recently that they have no accurate way to forecast an endgame to the war, CNBC reports .

So goes the global economy, so goes the International Criminal Court: The Trump administration is preparing to sanction the ICC into oblivion for indicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his crimes in Gaza, the Wall Street Journal reports

Germany’s socialists owe Berlin victory to radical housing affordability plan: Left-wing party Die Linke isn’t focused on permitting reform, or mandating a certain number of affordable units for new luxury apartment buildings, or giving tax breaks to real estate developers, or any of the other solutions to housing unaffordability you hear in Seattle, even from our socialist mayor. Instead, the party, which just came in first in Berlin’s state elections, plans to seize 220,000 apartments from large real estate corporations and let people live in them cheaply. The corporations will be compensated for the real estate (as the Winter Palace’s walls are holding for now) but, at the very least, it shows that voters respond to radical solutions.

Pussy Riot member spied for Putin, poorly: Rita Flores, who has since fled Russia, says she was threatened and blackmailed into becoming an informant for the FSB, spying and reporting on other anti-government artists. She does not appear to have been a particularly good one though. According to The Guardian , “Flores said she was not supposed to tell anyone about her recruitment, but immediately told ‘about 20 people’, putting it down to the fact she is a ‘massive gossip’.”

In ale gasn vu men geyt hert men zabostovkes: Pussy Riot grew out of another Russian avant-garde political group, Voina, who at times have been a bit more extreme. In 2011 , they ran a campaign to kiss as many Russian cops as possible, which would get you immediately shot in America, and there’s a recording of their efforts set to an old Yiddish pro-labor, anti-tsarist song conducted by Zalmen Mlotek.

articles.title: Wilson Seeks to Clean House Ahead of First Budget Rollout
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Friday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order intended to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the City’s operations while fostering the sustainability of its budget.

The executive order calls for the establishment of a cross-departmental work group that will work to strengthen the City’s operations and improve both the effectiveness and efficiency of the services it provides. The interdepartmental team is charged with delivering a set of recommendations of how to accomplish this by March 30th of next year.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

The list of possible topics for the team to discuss includes outcome-based budget evaluations, ways to streamline and track capital projects, implementing modern technology and money management practices, practicing risk management, and improving the City’s customer service.
“We live in a time right now where trust in government and institutions generally is very, very low,” Wilson said. “So, I believe that we really need to show that we can deliver.”

City Finance Director Dwight Dively, who held the position of Finance Director for the City for more than a decade before leaving for a 16-year stint as the director of King County's Office of Performance, Strategy and Budget, returned to work for the City earlier this year. Dively didn’t mince words about what he found upon his return.

"I left a city government that ran well," Dively said in a press release. "Coming back, I was struck by how much had changed, and not for the better. There is real work to do here, and I am glad to be part of doing it. Seattle residents trust us with their money and their services. Being a responsible steward of that trust is the job."

When The Urbanist asked for examples of current inefficiencies, Dively shared that right now, each City department has their own travel system, instead of utilizing a city-wide system that could both provide organizational discounts and more accountability. Another example mentioned was a lack of uniformity in the City trying to collect payments from insurance when a member of the public damages a City vehicle. Dively said that King County increased revenue more than $1 million per year through this practice.

City Budget Office Director Aly Pennucci offered another example, saying that some community service providers have contracts with multiple City departments. Having one streamlined contract per service provider would be more efficient for everyone.

Part of the work called for in the executive order will be ensuring the City has the right systems and technologies in place to optimize for efficiencies, whether that’s improving the experience of using the Find It, Fix It app, updating accounting rules, or making sure the Seattle Police Department is effectively tracking its officers’ overtime.

Dively told The Urbanist that the City doesn’t currently have an enterprise risk management program, which involves identifying the biggest risks in each department in order to manage those risks more effectively.
“In my opinion, we could save millions, if not tens of millions, of dollars every year, if we did [risk management] effectively,” Dively said.

A structural deficit has loomed over the City for the past several years, with the Jumpstart payroll tax acting as the primary means of closing the gap on a year-by-year basis. The estimated deficit for 2027 stood at $175 million .

However, as part of beginning the work to improve city governance, Wilson said that her new proposed budget being released on Tuesday doesn’t have a projected deficit in either the general fund or the Jumpstart fund through 2030.

“Coming into the Mayor's Office, I was very aware that we were facing a structural deficit and that we could not keep lurching from shortfall to shortfall, year after year,” Wilson said. “As mayor, I am very committed to taking comprehensive action, not just to balance the budget for the next biennium, but to ensure the longer-term fiscal health of our city.”

Wilson served on the Seattle Revenue Stabilization Workgroup in 2023, a group that looked into new revenue options for the City, and she ran on a platform of being willing to raise new progressive revenue to continue providing City services. However, most of the options on the table for new progressive revenue, including a city-wide capital gains tax, cannot be implemented immediately, with the majority requiring action by the state legislature before they can be adopted.

“[The Mayor] will be transmitting a budget that is making big strides towards sustainability but doesn't solve all of the problems,” Pennucci said. “And one of the things that's been really clear to me in coming back to the City and and working on the budget from the executive branch is that we really need better tools and resources to support a more dynamic budget process that's really focused on how are we getting the best value out of every public dollar, and it needs to be more outcome focused.”

Pennucci shared that in developing the 2027-2028 biennial budget, the office tried to better align budgets to actual spending, looking at budget areas where there has been regular underspend and long term vacancies in order to stretch the City’s dollars further.

The executive order also suggests implementing outcomes-based budget evaluations, which will be led by the Innovation and Performance team in the City budget office. This approach could involve examining all city programs in a specific space to see which ones are having better outcomes, whether there is any overlap between programs, and whether it makes sense to put more money into fewer programs or spread the resources out among many.

Pennucci said her office wants to think carefully about how to measure performance and not use only quantitative methods. In order to do justice to the work, the office plans to only pick one or two program areas to start. Wilson added that it’s important to avoid being simplistic in measuring outcomes.
Wilson did agree that she would be willing to cut programs that aren’t effective.

“We're not talking about trying to whittle down the size of government,” Wilson said. “We're talking about, if we're evaluating programs and we're like: this is the way to solve this problem, then maybe it makes sense to shift some resources from other programs that aren't performing as well into expanding that, and that's just a value question.”

Wilson has spoken before about wanting to show that progressive governance can work, a value she shares with New York Mayor and fellow socialist Zohran Mamdani. Both mayors have evoked allusions to sewer socialism, a movement that focuses on improving public services.

In the first eight months of her term, Wilson has focused on several priorities aimed at improving public services and addressing affordability, including passing a large library levy , putting a transit measure onto the November ballot that would boost frequency on several bus routes, banning junk fees for renters, providing universal school meals , and developing legislation that would ban surveillance pricing on groceries .

Meanwhile, Seattle received the top ranking from The Athletic for its hosting of the World Cup this summer, had no homicides in the month of July , and had its busiest month of visitor foot traffic downtown – in August – since 2019. And Denny Way now has a new bus lane to speed up Route 8, a move applauded by urbanists.

At the same time, Wilson has had her challenges. She’s been criticized for pausing the installation of more surveillance cameras and failing to build a productive relationship with the City Council. She walked back her proposal for a two-year break on builder fees , and she’s had to scale back her goal of opening 4,000 new shelter beds during her first term. Her administration was lambasted by the media for several weeks after a delay in communicating to the public in the aftermath of the Bite of Seattle shooting, even though it appears that SPD held the greater responsibility for the confusion . And her decision to ask SPD’s former Chief Shon Barnes to resign was not universally popular.
This executive order places the focus back on the nuts and bolts of City government, which appear to have been neglected in recent years.
“Some of the very basic things that any organization, whether it's a government, a nonprofit, a business, needs to do well, we don't do well anymore,” Dively said.

Dively said that in addition to saving or reprioritizing dollars, this executive order will set into motion work to ensure the City is complying with all relevant rules and optimizing the resources it has.

Wilson said she wants to use every City dollar as effectively as possible, leaning into efficiency and fiscal responsibility. She knows those terms are generally right-coded but wants to show how they can be brought to bear by a progressive administration to yield positive results.

“For a long time [those terms have] often been used to mean something else,” Wilson said. “Starving government so that it doesn't actually function well, cutting safety net programs, and we're seeing maybe an extreme version of this with the Trump administration, kind of the reductio ad absurdum of this ideology, where you have [...] extreme fiscal irresponsibility paired with slashing services in the most cruel manner and really dismantling important parts of the government apparatus. So I believe that progressive cities like Seattle have both an opportunity and really a responsibility to lead in the other direction.”

The introduction of Wilson’s proposed 2027-2028 budget on Tuesday will kick off two months of discussion as city councilmembers debate what changes they wish to make to the proposal. Given elevated tensions between the Mayor’s Office and City Council, it might prove to be a contentious budget season.
The City Council will need to pass a balanced budget before the end of the year, although they generally make their final budget vote before Thanksgiving.
“This behind-the-scenes work is not flashy,” Wilson said. “But I am committed to leaving city government in better shape than I found it."

articles.title: Housing Advocates, Workers Pack City Hall to Support Temporary Fee Break
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle councilmembers attending a rare late Friday afternoon meeting of the housing committee were met with an overflow crowd last week, and heard over an hour of testimony almost entirely in favor of a temporary discount on housing fees levied on builders. The "Housing Accelerator" proposal, put forward by committee chair Dionne Foster after months of behind-the-scenes negotiations, is intended to rescue a city development pipeline that has all but dried up.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Alongside builders and architects who spent their one minute of testimony laying out the bleak picture of Seattle's current development market were dozens of members of the city's construction trades. Donning hard hats and bright yellow vests, many held up signs that read "Proud YIMBY!" – directly referencing the Yes In By Backyard movement that champions the idea of reducing barriers to market-rate development.

Over the past two years, Seattle has seen a 26% decline in multifamily permitting, in contrast with a 31% increase seen statewide. Those diverging trends have dropped Seattle's share of statewide multifamily permits from 28% in 2024 to 16% now. Those red-alert statistics were presented to the committee by Michael Wilkerson, Director of Economic Research at ECOnorthwest, spelling out the need for a course correction from policymakers.

Under Foster's draft bill, a small constellation of building projects that have already had their permits vested would have access to a 80% discount in fees charged under the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) program – provided they can demonstrate "substantial progress" on construction within two years. The ordinance defines this milestone as passing the first foundation inspection.

New projects entering the pipeline can receive a 60% discount, and will have three years to get to substantial progress, but only if they address the city's relative shortage of family-sized apartments by including at least 25% of units with at least two bedrooms.

New projects do not have the same access to MHA discounts in neighborhoods deemed high risk of displacement, which include Chinatown International District, the Central District, Beacon Hill and urban centers up and down the Rainier Valley. A "legacy homeowner" exception would still grant the discount in those areas if the project site remains in community hands, rather than selling off to an outside developer.

"When a client walks into my office with a desire to build housing on a piece of property and the will to go forward, these days I start that conversation with the absolute certainty that I can get them a permit, I can design their building and they can build it, and if they do that, they will lose money," David Neiman, a partner with Neiman Taber Architects, said during Friday's testimony. "That is an unprecedented situation that I have never seen before in my career."

The hope is that by lowering one major cost component that the city has direct control over will allow more projects will be able to pencil – and bring more frontline construction workers back to jobsites. Developers backing the proposal say they have identified more than 30 stalled projects with vested permits that are ready to deliver more than 6,000 homes should the fee break be enacted, clearing their path to financing.

"We have well over a thousand folks out of work. We haven't seen those numbers since the last recession. So just anything that we can do to spur development, get folks back to work," Billy Hetherington, Political Director for Laborers' Local Union (LiUNA) 242, told The Urbanist . "MHA, the way it's designed, if there's nothing being built, it's not bringing in any money. So, taking a thoughtful reset and looking what happens during that reset, and trying to look at the policy again here in a year or two years to fit it to the right economic climate we're in."
Comments Friday were not universally in support, with some concerns raised about reducing a dedicated revenue source for affordable housing.

"Reducing the City's only housing affordability program is the wrong lever to remove," Alexandra Johnson of the Duwamish River Community Coalition told councilmembers. "MHA, by the City's own study, was 3-5% of total developer costs, and permitting, design reviews, including delays from the city were 9-11%. Rather than committing to reforming internal systems and prioritizing progressive recalibrations of MHA – very similar to what the mayor's taskforce on housing will commit to solving – the city is choosing the least equitable route and a verified ineffective route by the City's own analysis."
So far the proposal appears to have broad support on the council, with Council President Joy Hollingsworth signing on as a co-sponsor.

"The one thing that really stands out the most to me has been the numbers and the data and the hard facts," Hollingsworth said. "My four goals during this process: build more housing, all of it; keep affordable housing in our city as well, to protect those sustainable pathways and funding and operations, long term; protect neighborhoods with high level of risk or displacement; and then also incentivize family-size housing and units. And that's a very thin line to try to navigate. So I really appreciate this conversation."

Paired with the ordinance, which could get a vote as soon as early January, is a companion resolution that has rankled some of the biggest proponents of a potential MHA reduction. It would state the council's intent to study whether the MHA program should be expanded to the city's Neighborhood Residential zones – the formerly single family neighborhoods where a state-mandated upzone unlocked additional density last year.

"I'm trying to set the stage for what our long-term approach looks like. And if you look at the language in the resolution, what you'll see is some significant guardrails in there, including specific language that says we want to direct central staff to develop this in such a way that it does not have a substantial negative impact on development in this area," Foster told The Urbanist following Friday's meeting. "My intent is not to kill housing projects. My intent is housing production and the long-term stability of this funding source in a way that makes sense for the future of our city."

With no MHA fees in place in NR zones but significantly more development capacity, builders often have an incentive to advance a project there rather than in a low-rise (LR) zone closer to transit and amenities, where MHA fees would apply. That disparity, land use committee chair Eddie Lin told The Urbanist, is one reason that he's expressing support for the proposed resolution.

"I think it's worth exploring. I don't see the resolution as a final decision," Lin said. "I think there's some interesting nuances that we could get into there in terms of encouraging greater density. Like, do we encourage lower fees for greater density? Do we look at things like homeowners who might be building for themselves? And so there's a lot to unpack. I just see this as the start of the conversation in trying to build the information that we would need to have a more thoughtful discussion."

With committee work on hold until after Thanksgiving for a full-time focus on the city budget, the Housing Accelerator (with its trailer resolution) is set to come back for additional discussions in December. By that time, the housing committee will have a new member, with District 5 Councilmember Debora Juarez stepping down as soon as special election results in that district are certified.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Gregoire and Locke Speak for Oligarchs, Not the Democratic Base
articles.author: John Burbank (Guest Contributor)
paras: Unfortunately, the mainstream media is trumpeting the missives of former Governors Gary Locke and Christine Gregoire to cut progressive policymakers off at the knees. The Seattle Times characterizes Gregoire’s and Locke’s criticism as an “intervention” – as if Democrats have an addiction. They want to focus on “out-of-control” revenue and taxes, and not on the services that are provided by our government.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

When Locke and Gregoire were governors, Washington state did not have paid family and medical leave for workers, we did not have long term care, we did not have the climate commitment act that funds projects to limit greenhouse emissions in our state.

Gregoire wrote budgets that doubled tuition at the University of Washington, which under her leadership exceeded $10,500 in 2011 ($16,000 in today’s dollars), eliminated Basic Health for low-income Washingtonians, almost completely defunded our public parks, and suspended initiatives which had been passed by the people into law to reduce K-12 class sizes and increase teacher pay. And now she works for the corporate oligarchs who fund her business policy alliance, Challenge Seattle .

Governor Locke began his own attack on public services at an Association of Washington Business conference. These two old-time leaders don’t speak for Democrats, they speak for the oligarchy. And it’s important Washington raises its voice for the people, rather than doing the bidding of oligarchs.

The upcoming Congressional elections and the probability that Democrats will win majorities in the House and the Senate is grabbing much of our political attention. These majorities, whether dominated by mainstream or progressive Democrats, could effectively decelerate the undermining of our democracy.

But we need to be aware of Trump’s veto power and the fact that whatever the legal outcomes, the Trump administration will continue to roll over them, with the help of the Supreme Court. Don't get me wrong - these elections are extremely important and I, as millions of other Americans, have contributed significantly to help our allies win political power.

But, we must not forget about legislative elections in our own state. While we may be unable to reverse oligarchic neoliberalism at the federal level, we can build our own universally shared commonwealth in Washington state. In fact, we must do so, to provide a template for rebuilding our country, not as it was before Trump, but as it should be as a true democracy, inclusive of social democracy. This is fundamental to saving our country.

Progressive states can go on the offensive, embodying a counterpoint to the growing fascism of Trump and his accolades, as well as to the neoliberal planned disintegration of public services embraced by Republicans and many Democrats.

Rather than bemoaning state budget increases, we should be looking at people’s needs. But the current Democratic budget architects have actually taken away support for these needs. These legislators have defunded child care, reduced College Grants for low-income and working class students, cut $27 million out of “transition to kindergarten” programs, and chopped 10% out of the Parent to Parent program , a vital connection for parents of children with developmental disabilities.
That is just a start. The legislature managed nickel and dime (or better said, million and million) cuts to programs across the board. These cuts hurt all of us.

When legislators convene in January, they must look forward, not back. They must step up to all the cuts coming down from the Trump administration – possibly $15 billion over the next decade - as well as the unmet needs which have been left unfunded for decades. We must build our commonwealth. Let’s consider the bookends for K-12 education, child care and higher education.

21 years ago the Legislature established a career and wage ladder for child care teachers . However, as part of Gregoire’s cost cutting, they stopped funding this ladder in 2011. The median wage in 2025 for child care workers in our state was $20.55 and the career and wage ladder law lies dormant. It doesn’t need a new law – it is ready to be funded and could create a true and respected career ladder for 30,000 child care teachers. That would cost $1 billion a year .

Child care is a budget buster for working parents. In New Mexico, it isn’t. That is because the state of New Mexico provides universal no-cost childcare for the children of all residents. If we did the same thing, the cost is estimated at $2.5 billion a year. A universal child care program voids all of the Legislature’s cost-cutting antics, like the $143 million cut to Working Connections Child Care and throwing off kids from child care by lowering the income ceiling for eligibility.

Tuition and living expenses at the University of Washington exceed $37,000 for in-state students and almost $30,000 at Seattle Central Community College . At Evergreen State College tuition itself is a little under $9,000. But not if you are a graduating senior from Shelton High School. All Shelton graduates, regardless of income, get four years of tuition-free education at Evergreen, plus help with the cost of living. In September of 2024, three students from Shelton enrolled at Evergreen. In September 2025, 53 students enrolled. Their retention rate is 95%. And this month 60 new Shelton high school graduates will be enrolling at Evergreen.

This pilot project points to the fact that it is the cost of tuition, more than anything else, which is keeping kids from going to college. Washington state’s Business Roundtable , again representing the top corporate oligarchs, claim they want to increase post-high school enrollment to 70%. Currently only 53% of last year’s high school graduates are enrolled in higher education. But these oligarchs don’t want to fund higher education.

Amazon and Microsoft in particular benefit from a tax ceiling legislated for them, only. No other businesses benefit. The workforce education investment fund loses over $1 billion a year from this giveaway. With that funding the state could have tuition-free education for all community colleges and regional universities, and half the tuition at UW and WSU. That would be a true gamechanger for students, their families, and our economy.

Between child care and higher education alone, the state needs to raise an additional $5 billion a year. Where is that money? About 1,900 households in our state enjoy incomes exceeding $5 million. A 10% tax would bring in about $1.5 billion. A half of a percent tax on wealth would generate at least $3 billion a year. A 5% tax on compensation in excess of the Social Security tax ceiling tax ($184,500) would generate another $3 billion a year.

We must tax the oligarchs, the merely wealthy, and the corporations that have been Trump’s toadies and beneficiaries. It is of public and private benefit to tax these corporate behemoths and C-suite executives, including all those privileged “workers” who are granted salaries in excess of a million dollars, 60 times the minimum wage and more than 13 times the median salary in our state.

Runaway salaries pull the beneficiaries away from the body politic and the culture of community. Families with incomes exceeding a million dollars segregate their kids in private schools, surround themselves with private clubs, inculcate themselves and their kids with a sense of superiority, and stand apart from the financial stresses and realities faced by 90% of the population. Many of them get public gratitude for charitable contributions while corrupting the potential for common wellbeing.

We need this new revenue to rebuild our public services and make up for the billions of dollars of cuts coming down from the Trump Administration. We need progressive taxation to build the cross-class solidarity of our state. E Pluribus Unum .

articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle Needs More Than a 10-Minute Walk or Roll to a Park
articles.author: Rebecca Bear
paras: Seattle is nationally and internationally recognized for its park system. By one widely cited metric, nearly 99% of residents live within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park. That achievement deserves recognition; ensuring that almost everyone lives near green space is an important planning goal, and one the City should continue to prioritize.

But proximity is only part of the story. As Seattle plans for significant population growth under the Comprehensive Plan, we should ask a harder question: Is park space equitable, accessible, or equipped to serve kids and families who rely on it?
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

A park can be within a 10-minute walk or roll and still be difficult or unsafe to reach because of dangerous intersections, steep terrain, missing sidewalks, or barriers created by major roads and industrial corridors. This is especially important in the Duwamish Valley, where highways, freight routes, rail lines, and industrial land uses can separate neighborhoods from nearby open space.

Seattle’s parks can also be overcrowded, inaccessible to people with disabilities, culturally unwelcoming, or lacking in basic amenities like bathrooms, sports fields, shade/tree canopy, playgrounds, barbecues, benches, and tables. Under today's standard, these parks still count in the walk score even if they fall short of meeting the needs of the surrounding neighborhood. The same report that highlights Seattle’s high number of residents living within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park also shows that access to parks is not distributed equally.

Residents in neighborhoods of color have 32% less park space per person than residents in predominantly White neighborhoods. Residents in low-income neighborhoods have 51% less park space per person than those in higher-income neighborhoods. Meanwhile, Seattle ranks near the bottom among the nation's 100 largest cities for several park amenities, including sports fields, recreation centers, bathrooms, and basketball courts.

None of these shortcomings are captured by that 10-minute walk measurement. Seattle should ask whether residents can safely reach parks, whether those parks provide the amenities families need, and whether investments are reaching neighborhoods that have historically had fewer high-quality recreational opportunities.

Take the South Park Community Center, which requires crossing the highway on one of the few footpaths to reach the area and offers an opportunity for additional tree shade around the turf field and playground. The metric also fails to tell us whether the park system is keeping pace with population growth. Seattle currently provides about 8.3 acres of parkland for every 1,000 residents. Other growing, high-density cities provide substantially more. Denver offers approximately 9.9 acres per 1,000 residents, Washington, D.C. provides 11.8, and Minneapolis offers 12.3.
As Seattle welcomes more neighbors, existing parks will serve more people. That is good for city life, but only if our public spaces are resourced and growing alongside our housing.
Fortunately, this is not an either-or choice.

The City should pair the existing metric with measures that answer different, equally important questions. How much park space is available for the people who live nearby? Are parks accessible to people of all ages and abilities? Are they in good condition? Is there access to natural features like trees or water? Do they have the amenities communities actually need? Are they becoming overcrowded and run down as neighborhoods grow?

Together, these measures would give policymakers a much clearer picture of where investments are needed most. This approach is especially important because Seattle's Comprehensive Plan is designed to accommodate substantial housing growth over the coming decades. New housing should be accompanied by investments in parks and public spaces so that growth improves quality of life rather than putting additional strain on the places where residents already live. Housing and green space should not compete with one another. They should be planned together. Communities deserve both!

A growing city needs more homes AND more places for children to play, neighbors to gather, seniors to exercise, and families to find respite from summer heat or Seattle rain. These experiences are not luxuries; they are part of the infrastructure that makes urban living healthy, resilient, and equitable.

Seattle has every reason to celebrate that nearly every resident lives within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park. But we can’t stop there. The next step is making sure all neighborhoods have parks that are large enough, welcoming enough, and well-equipped enough to serve the city we are becoming.

We need to measure not only whether a park is nearby, but also if it is truly thriving, both for itself and the community it serves. Park access is an issue of environmental justice, public health, and who gets to thrive in Seattle. As the city grows, we have an opportunity to make sure that growth does not deepen existing disparities, but instead helps repair them. Every neighborhood deserves not just a park within a 10-minute walk, but a park that is safe, accessible, welcoming, well-maintained, and truly worthy of the community it serves.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent

paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. articles.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support.

Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing .

The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware.
“I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said.
State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session.

Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime.

“Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.”
Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”
“More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said.

ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising.

“We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.”
In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag.

Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies.

Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.”

Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said.

It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts.

Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May.
The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.

Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote.
The post Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting appeared first on ProPublica .

paras: Kitsap Transit’s Fall 2026 service change began yesterday, September 12. This service change is also introducing a new pilot route, SK Ride Express, to connect McCormick Woods and McCormick Village to the Port Orchard Foot Ferry. articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
